frontmatter.title: Bank Raya: digital growth, sub-cost-of-capital returns
frontmatter.summary: We initiate with SELL and a Rp9 target, -91.1% from the Rp105 price. The market pays 0.9x book for a bank whose FY2025 was a loss and whose clean-up-normalised ROE never reaches 4.7% against a 13.0% cost of equity, which on the house warranted-multiple formula is 0.08x book. Growth is real; earnings power is not.
thesis: The FY2025 loss was a balance-sheet event, not a one-off: provisions of IDR553.6bn and a deferred-tax write-off of IDR176.9bn took the year to a loss of IDR-498.6bn; the allowance has since fallen to IDR634.8bn and gross NPL to 2.5% [S7][S8][S3].

The 2026 profit is recovery income, not franchise earnings: IDR276.7bn of recovery income in nine months against profit before tax of IDR7.3bn for the full year; strip the recovery line and the nine months are a loss [S7].

Digital is growing but from a small base and at a cost: digital outstanding of IDR3,040.0bn sits inside a total book that has shrunk to IDR6,468.8bn as legacy lending is worked out, and fee income is only IDR8.1bn in nine months [S7][S3].

Capital is the option the base case cannot bank: a CAR of 42.4% against risk assets far smaller than equity leaves a large surplus, but IDR3,255.6bn of accumulated losses bars any distribution and no capital reduction has been announced [S3][S7][S8][S6].
At Rp105 the stock still trades at 0.9x book, which requires a sustainable ROE near the 13.0% cost of equity; we model 4.8% and value the equity at Rp6 a share.

blocks.text: **SELL, target Rp9 (-91.1% from Rp105).** Bank Raya is the smallest listed leg of BRI Group's digital strategy, and the stock is already near its 103.0 low against a 254.0 high: most of the de-rating has happened. It still carries 0.9x book for a bank that lost IDR-498.6bn in FY2025 and that in our base case reaches 4.5% only by FY2030E and 4.7% by FY2035E — below the 13.0% cost of equity a minority holder should demand [S7][S8].

The variant view is not that the digital franchise is fake. Digital outstanding has grown to IDR3,040.0bn, CASA is 35.8%, and the app now carries 4.9 mm transactions a year [S3][S4]. The variant view is that the clean-up has consumed the profit pool that was supposed to fund the transition: the FY2025 loss came from IDR553.6bn of provisions plus a IDR176.9bn deferred-tax write-off [S8], and the FY2026 profit is carried by IDR276.7bn of recovery income in nine months [S7]. Strip the recovery line out and the nine months are a loss, not a break-even: the IDR7.3bn full-year result we forecast exists only because that one line is larger than the profit. Two thirds of the revenue base is interest income on a balance sheet whose earning assets earn a spread the cost base and the provisions consume.

The multiple is not a capitulation multiple. At 0.9x book the stock is not cheap against the deepest-discount small digital peers in the house screen: BBYB, BACA and BABP all trade below half of book, while ARTO and BANK trade much closer to AGRO's own multiple, so the peer discount is not uniform [S0]. A reader can therefore hold two things at once: the price has fallen a long way, and it still embeds a franchise return the accounts do not show. Our target is what the accounts support; the bull case, at Rp20, is what a proven franchise alone would be worth, and even that is below book. It excludes any capital-return action, which section five explains would be worth several times the bull target.

Three things move the value. First, the loan book: it fell to IDR6,468.8bn at September 2026 as the legacy book was worked out [S7], and our base case has it roughly flat through FY2027E before digital growth resumes. Second, the cost of risk: gross NPL fell from 14.0% to 2.5% in nine months [S9][S3], but the low-quality loan stock is still 19.3% of the book and IDR1,087.3bn is restructured [S7]. Third, capital: a 42.4% CAR means the bank does not need equity, but it also means most of the equity is not needed by the risk assets — and with IDR3,255.6bn of accumulated losses still on the balance sheet it cannot be distributed without a shareholder resolution [S7][S8].

The link between a bank's return on equity and its price-to-book is one of the oldest identities in
bank analysis: a bank that earns less than its cost of equity should trade below book, and the gap
widens with the difference. What makes Indonesian digital banks difficult to frame is that the market
often pays for the option on a future franchise rather than for current returns. Our method values the
current franchise and puts the option in the bull case, where the reader can see what has to be true.

Bank Raya is a national commercial bank listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange under the AGRO ticker. It was founded as PT Bank Agroniaga in 1989, listed in 2003, renamed PT Bank Rakyat Indonesia Agroniaga in 2012 after BRI became the controlling shareholder, and now operates as PT Bank Raya Indonesia Tbk [S9]. BRI owns 86.8% of the shares [S7]; the public holds the rest, with a free float of about 12.9% of the share count [S0]. It reports in rupiah, employs 766 people [S0], and consolidates no material subsidiary.

The business model is a small commercial bank being rebuilt around digital distribution inside the BRI ecosystem. Management describes the role as BRI Group's "digital attacker" for micro, small and medium enterprises, with the widest online-to-offline network in the country — services reachable through 1.9 mm access points, including BRILink agents, CRM units, ATMs and BRI branches [S9]. Lending is organised around three named products: Pinang Dana Talangan to BRILink and Pegadaian agents, Pinang Flexi to payroll-based employees, and Pinang Maksima to business owners against invoices [S9]. On the funding side the bank runs digital savings and current accounts through the Raya app, alongside time deposits and the legacy branch book [S9].

The mix has moved decisively toward digital lending. Digital outstanding was 39.8% of the loan book at end-FY2025, up from roughly a third a year earlier [S9], and had reached IDR3,040.0bn by September 2026 [S3] while the total book shrank to IDR6,468.8bn [S7]. Funding mix has improved with it: CASA reached 35.8% at September 2026 from 33.6% at end-FY2025 [S3][S9], and digital savings alone were IDR2,400.0bn [S4]. Deposits were IDR9,540.0bn at end-FY2025 [S9] and the loan-to-deposit ratio is 78.1% on our forecast [S7]. The bank is liquid and lightly levered: securities and placements are a large share of the balance sheet, and the liquidity ratios are far above the regulatory minimum [S5].

Strategy is stated as "exploit and explore": exploit the BRI ecosystem for distribution and funding, and explore partnerships outside it to widen reach [S5]. That is a sensible plan for a bank of this size, and it is also the source of the governance question in the final section: the ecosystem that makes the franchise viable is the same group that controls it. Management changed at the October 2026 RUPSLB [S6], and the new team inherits a smaller, cleaner book and a capital ratio the market treats as optionality.

Competitively, Bank Raya is a challenger with a thin franchise. It is one of the smallest listed commercial banks in Indonesia by assets [S0], it has no corporate franchise, and its deposit base is narrow relative to the large banks [S7]. Its one durable advantage is BRI's distribution: 1.9 mm access points and the BRILink agent network give it a customer acquisition channel that standalone digital banks have to buy [S9]. Against that, the brand is not a deposit magnet on its own, and the products — small-ticket working-capital loans to agents and micro-merchants — are exactly where competition from fintech lenders and the other digital banks is most intense [S12].

Indonesian banking entered 2026 in a liquidity-rich, margin-poor phase. Bank Umum loan growth slowed to 9.5% in 2025 from a double-digit rate the year before, asset growth was 9.5%, deposit growth was 13.8%, and system gross NPL held at 2.0% [S9]. Deposits growing faster than loans is the important fact for this report: when the system is funded faster than it can lend, competition for assets compresses loan yields while deposit costs reprice down only slowly, and every bank's NIM is squeezed [S9]. A small bank with a narrow deposit franchise feels that squeeze first.

The digital-bank segment is where the growth and the risk sit. OJK describes four routes by which digital banks have been created, including the acquisition of a small bank by one of the largest banking groups and its transformation into a digital lender [S12] — the route BRI took with this bank. The regulator's message in September 2026 was pointed: an ecosystem advantage must be built into a business model that can grow sustainably and must not depend solely on affiliate support [S12]. That is a direct challenge to banks whose distribution, funding and customer base all come from a parent, and it is the single most important regulatory statement for AGRO in the archive.

Competition in digital banking is now crowded and price-led. The listed digital challengers — the Jago, Neo Commerce, DNAR, Balé, Superbank and SeaBank platforms — compete for the same mass-affluent and micro-merchant customer, and most are funded by a parent or a technology partner. The product set is easy to copy — savings, e-wallet top-ups, small working-capital loans — so differentiation comes from distribution and data, not from features. Bank Raya's distribution advantage through BRILink agents is real but rented from its parent, which is why the OJK statement matters more here than for a standalone bank [S9][S12].

The house macro deck points the same way. Its regime call on Indonesian rate-sensitive banks is to avoid the NIM story: with Bank Indonesia at a policy rate the deck treats as flat and inflation near target, the sector's margin recovery depends on deposit repricing rather than on loan yields, and the small CASA-poor banks are last in the queue. We do not import the deck's rates into this model — the NIM path is built bottom-up from the bank's own mix and is stated as such in section three — but the direction agrees with our conclusion, and we reference it rather than claiming independent support [S9].

The five forces are unfavourable. Rivalry is high and rising, because credit products are homogeneous and the digital banks are all chasing the same borrowers. New entrants are still arriving through the acquisition route OJK describes [S12]. The power of depositors is high: the system's deposit growth outran loan growth in 2025 [S9], but the marginal depositor is rate-sensitive and can move to a higher-paying platform in minutes. Buyer power is moderate — micro-borrowers have few formal alternatives, but fintech lenders and paylater products are close substitutes. Substitutes are strong: e-wallet credit, paylater and peer-to-peer lending take exactly the small-ticket, short-tenor borrower this bank targets.

Regulation cuts both ways. The digital-bank framework that allowed this transformation also imposes capital and governance obligations that a sub-scale bank struggles to meet, and OJK has shifted its focus from accelerating digitalisation to demanding sustainable business models [S12]. For a bank with a capital ratio of 42.4% [S3], capital is not the binding constraint today; the binding constraint is proving that the model can earn a return on that capital without leaning on the parent.

The moat is thin and conditional. What Bank Raya owns is a banking licence, a deposit franchise of IDR9,540.0bn [S9], and access to BRI's distribution [S9]. What it does not own is pricing power, a proprietary data advantage, or a customer relationship that survives a better offer. We therefore treat the franchise as a distribution asset inside BRI Group rather than as a standalone franchise, and we do not pay for growth beyond what the balance sheet and the deposit base can fund.

The reported history is dominated by two years of balance-sheet repair. In FY2024 the bank earned IDR50.9bn, but that profit rested on IDR536.0bn of non-interest income — itself mostly recoveries of written-off loans — against pre-provision profit of IDR483.8bn [S8]. In FY2025 the same book produced a loss of IDR-498.6bn: provisions rose to IDR553.6bn and a IDR176.9bn deferred-tax write-off followed, taking profit before tax to IDR-321.7bn [S8]. The loss was a clean-up, not a trading accident, and the NPL ratio at the end of that year — 14.0% gross against a management target of a few per cent — says how large the legacy problem was [S9].

The clean-up continued through FY2026. The loan-loss allowance on loans fell from IDR1,442.2bn at end-FY2025 to IDR634.8bn at September 2026 as legacy loans were written off against it [S7]. Gross NPL fell to 2.5% and net NPL to 0.4% [S3], while the low-quality loan stock was still 19.3% of the book and IDR1,087.3bn of loans remained restructured [S7]. The nine months carried IDR295.7bn of impairment and still produced a profit before tax of IDR21.0bn [S7]. That profit is the whole argument of this report in one line: the recovery line in non-interest income is larger than pre-tax profit, so without it the nine months are a loss of roughly the size of the FY2025 loss, not a break-even [S7]. We take the nine-month run-rate as the starting point for FY2026E, which is why our full-year forecast is a small profit of IDR7.3bn rather than the loss the first version of this note carried.

Earnings quality is the crux of the investment case, and the flags are mixed. On the positive side, the bank has disclosed the clean-up, the FY2025 accounts were audited without qualification, and the allowance is now a plausible proportion of the impaired book [S8][S7]. On the negative side, the FY2026 profit depends on recovery income: IDR276.7bn in the P&L for nine months (IDR276.6bn in the cash-flow statement) against IDR125.1bn for all of FY2025 [S7][S8]. Recovery income is a real cash flow — it is collected from previously written-off borrowers — but it is not annuity income, and it swings violently: the FY2024 comparative was a multiple of the FY2025 figure [S8]. Fee income, the recurring part of non-interest income, is only IDR8.1bn in nine months, flat on the prior year [S7].

The disclosure does not let us size the pool. Neither the FY2025 accounts nor the nine-month statements state the written-off stock still available for recovery, so we cannot capitalise the run-rate with any confidence [S7][S8][S9]. We therefore normalise non-interest income instead: FY2026E annualises the nine-month run-rate, then the line runs off to roughly the FY2025 recovery level plus fee and securities income, and is held flat thereafter. That is a deliberate refusal to treat a finite pool as an annuity, and it is the single largest reason our terminal return is lower than the first version of this note showed. The bear case stops the recovery stream earlier; the bull case lets it persist.

The second quality flag is the way provisions and write-offs interact. Because the bank writes loans off against an allowance that was built in prior periods, the reported credit cost in any one year understates the economic loss on the book; the FY2025 charge is the correction, and the FY2026 release of allowance is the mirror image [S7]. This is disclosed and standard practice, so we classify it as optics rather than manipulation — but it is why we anchor the forecast on the stock of impaired loans (KKR and restructured) rather than on the reported credit-cost line alone [S7].

Margins are improving from a low base. Reported NIM was 5.8% in the first nine months of 2026, with interest expense down year on year as high-cost time deposits repriced [S7]. On our earning-asset base, NII of IDR711.3bn implies a margin of 5.9% for FY2026E, rising to 6.3% by FY2030E as digital loans and CASA take a larger share of the balance sheet [S7][S3]. The rate path is not from the house macro deck: we hold the policy rate flat and let the mix do the work, which is the conservative reading of a deck whose tilt on Indonesian rate-sensitive banks is negative. The NIM path is therefore a bottom-up judgement a reader can test, not an imported forecast.

The balance-sheet arithmetic matters here, so we state it. The template sets earning assets as loans times a ratio and total assets as the prior year grown at loan growth; the ratio must equal the last actual's total-assets-to-loans ratio or the two lines diverge. At December 2025 the bank had IDR13,087.1bn of assets against IDR7,715.3bn of loans, and we hold that ratio flat, so earning assets stay at almost the whole balance sheet and can never exceed it. The consequence is that with loans down -17.0% in FY2026E the model's total-assets proxy is smaller than the actual September 2026 balance sheet of IDR12,567.6bn [S7], where the securities and placement book absorbed the loan rundown. The FY2026E NII of IDR711.3bn is therefore lower than the nine-month run-rate annualises to; it is the right number for the balance sheet the model can articulate, and it is the number behind every valuation in section four.

The proxy has a visible limit, which we disclose rather than smooth. The template grows total assets at the loan-growth input and deposits at their own input, while equity accumulates retained profit; when loans fall faster than the equity base, the two paths stop reconciling. In FY2026E deposits of IDR8,204.4bn plus equity of IDR3,018.7bn come to more than the total-assets proxy of IDR10,862.3bn, so the residual other-liabilities line implied by the balance-sheet identity turns negative, against a positive residual in FY2025 (IDR9,540.0bn deposits, IDR3,011.3bn equity and IDR13,087.1bn total assets). The plug belongs to the template's asset proxy, not to the bank, and its effect on the valuation is nil: net interest income is built from the loan line times the earning-assets ratio, not from deposits; equity, ROE and book value are untouched; and the deposit path only sets the displayed loan-to-deposit ratio of 78.1%. We show the gap rather than force a deposit input that the September filing contradicts [S7].

Costs are the bank's other structural problem. Operating expenses were IDR638.8bn in FY2025 and IDR719.6bn in our FY2026E forecast, a cost-to-income ratio of 72.1% and 64.2% respectively [S7]. The reported nine-month cost-to-income ratio was 64.2% [S7], flattered by recovery income; on recurring income the ratio is far worse. The template scales operating expenses with total operating income at the assumed ratio, so a flat ratio means costs grow with revenue rather than with inflation. That is what the record shows — the nine-month cost base annualises above the FY2025 figure despite a flat headcount of 766 [S0][S7] — and we do not assume the branch and technology base shrinks, or that a sub-scale bank wins operating leverage it has not yet shown.

Capital and liquidity are strong, and that is the puzzle. Equity was IDR3,011.3bn at end-FY2025 and our FY2026E figure is IDR3,018.7bn [S7]; CAR is 42.4% [S3] against a risk-asset base that our model puts at 44.1% of loans in capital-ratio terms. The bank holds a large securities and placement book, and its liquidity ratios are well above the regulatory floor [S5]. But IDR3,255.6bn of accumulated losses sit inside that equity, the dividend is zero in our forecast, and no capital reduction has been announced [S7][S8][S6]. A bank with this much capital and this little return on it is either a capital-return story or a value trap; on the current record it is the latter, and the option on the former is priced in the bull case.

Our forecast is deliberately arithmetic rather than aspirational. Loans fall to IDR6,403.7bn in FY2026E as the legacy book is worked out, are roughly flat in FY2027E, then grow with digital at 11.0% to 12.0% [S7][S3]. That path overrides management's own FY2026 business-plan targets of loan growth of 5.0% at the bottom of its range, NIM above 5.0% and CASA of 35.0% [S9], and the override is a fact of the accounts rather than a view: gross loans fell from IDR7,715.3bn at December 2025 to IDR6,468.8bn at September 2026, a year-to-date contraction of about one sixth, while deposits fell by less, because the securities book absorbed the difference [S7]. The FY2026E assumption of -17.0% is our forecast for the full year, not a filing fact: it carries the nine-month rundown through the fourth quarter. FY2027E is the crossover year, digital grows from a small base, and the residual legacy book halves. Deposits follow a similar path, so the loan-to-deposit ratio stays near 78.1% before grinding up [S7]. NII grows from IDR711.3bn to IDR914.7bn on mix alone, non-interest income falls from its recovery-driven peak to IDR196.4bn, and credit cost falls from 5.6% to 2.8% as the digital book, kept below a few per cent NPL by management, becomes the majority of loans [S9][S7]. The result is an ROE path from 0.2% to 4.5% and 4.7% in the terminal year — a real improvement on a loss-making base, and still well below the cost of equity [S7].

Two data notes, both of which a reader rebuilding this from the filings will meet. First, the market data pack carries a net interest income and non-interest income split that differs from the audited LK: for FY2025 the pack shows NII of IDR712.6bn and the LK shows IDR696.3bn, with non-interest income IDR172.8bn against IDR167.2bn [S0][S8]. The engine restates loans, deposits, provisions, operating expenses, equity and the balance sheet from the facts, but its restatement list does not cover the two revenue lines, so the pack supplies that history. The difference is small and does not change the trend, the ROE path or the valuation, but it is disclosed rather than smoothed. Second, the LK states 24,740 mm shares [S8][S11] against the pack's much lower count; the restated count is used for EPS and book value per share throughout, while the pack's market-capitalisation field of 1,147,644,741,810.0 still uses its own count. On the LK count the market capitalisation is Rp105 times 24,740 mm shares — a reader should use that figure, not the pack's, and we use the corrected figure wherever market capitalisation matters.

A bank is valued on the relationship between its return on equity and its cost of equity, so we use justified price-to-book as the primary method and residual income as the check that prices the same fact year by year. The house card's digital-bank variant is explicit that residual income is inapplicable on near-zero earnings and that P/BV should be applied once the bank is profitable, with the base case starting from the rate most challengers never reach — the cost of equity [S7][S8]. That is exactly this bank's position. We give the dividend discount model no weight because the bank pays no dividend and cannot until accumulated losses are cleared [S8]. A PE-based cross-check is not meaningful at near-zero earnings, and a trailing P/B multiple simply restates the question.

The cost of equity is 13.0%. The engine build is the ten-year sovereign yield of 7.4%, less the 1.6% default spread, plus a beta of 0.90 times the sum of the mature-market equity risk premium (4.2%) and the country risk premium (2.5%), plus a 1.1% calibration premium [S0]. The premium pins the IDR build to the method card's sovereign-plus-equity-risk-premium approach for Indonesian banks rather than to an imported USD rate; with no debt in the capital structure, the cost of equity is also the discount rate. The peer on the same method set runs the unpinned build and therefore prices a little over a percentage point cheaper; we do not follow it, because the card's IDR band is where the premium puts us and the risk in this franchise is not lower than the peer's.

Justified P/B is 0.08x, or Rp10 a share. The arithmetic is unforgiving and the inputs are the whole argument. We set the sustainable ROE at 4.8%, which is the model's own terminal return — the FY2035E figure and the highest year in the forecast, with FY2030E at 4.5% [S7][S8]. The first version of this note used a flat override above every year the model produced, on an argument about a post-forecast mix shift that no source supported; it is withdrawn. Against a 13.0% cost of equity and 4.0% terminal growth, a sustainable ROE just under five per cent is worth a small fraction of book, and the multiple is knife-edge: a hundred basis points on the sustainable ROE moves it by roughly the same amount as the whole terminal growth assumption. We would rather show that fragility than hide it behind a round number.

Residual income gives Rp0 a share and carries 35% of the weight. It floors at zero because the bank's return is below the cost of equity in every year of the forecast, so the present value of the residual stream is negative and the engine's limited-liability rule caps it at zero. That is not an independent second opinion and we do not present it as one; it is the card's point restated, that a bank holding equity it does not need and earning less than its cost of equity on it destroys value every year it holds it.

The divergence between the methods is the most important judgement in this report, so we state it plainly. At a capital ratio of 42.4%, the equity the bank actually needs to support its risk assets is a fraction of the IDR3,011.3bn on the balance sheet [S3][S7]. The surplus is invested in securities and placements and earns a return below the cost of equity, which is exactly what residual income penalises. If that surplus were returned, the remaining franchise would earn a double-digit return on the capital it needs, and the stock would be worth far more than either method shows. We do not put that in the base case. The accumulated losses of IDR3,255.6bn bar a dividend [S7][S8], and no capital reduction, buyback or special distribution has been announced [S6] — but a capital reduction is a shareholder resolution rather than a distributable-profit test, and BRI's 86.8% control makes it executable. No source in this pack says otherwise, which is the honest position: the option is real, it is worth a large part of book, and it is entirely at the controlling shareholder's discretion. That is why it sits in the bull narrative and cannot be a probability-weighted bridge item: the engine does not let a bridge reach a bank valuation method, so we describe it and do not pretend to price it.

What does the market price imply? At Rp105, the stock trades at 0.9x book. For a bank with a 13.0% cost of equity and 4.0% growth, that multiple is consistent with a sustainable ROE at or above the cost of equity — roughly double the 4.8% we model. The market is therefore either pricing a full turnaround in returns or pricing the capital-return option. We think the first is optimistic on the evidence in the accounts, and the second is a corporate-action bet rather than an earnings bet [S7][S8]. The stock is at 103.0 against a 254.0 high, so the reader should note that most of the de-rating has already happened: this is not a call that the market has yet to discover the problem, it is a call that even the de-rated price still embeds a franchise return the accounts do not show. Three of the small digital peers — BBYB, BACA and BABP — trade below half of book, a deeper discount than AGRO's; but ARTO and BANK trade much closer to AGRO's own multiple, so relative value does not uniformly rescue the multiple either [S0].

The sensitivity table is the most honest page of this report. Moving NIM by sixty basis points or credit cost by sixty basis points moves the target by a few rupiah, because the bank's earnings are small relative to its equity and every one of those earnings scenarios leaves residual income at zero. The variables that matter are the sustainable ROE, the cost of equity and terminal growth, and they matter because the multiple is near its floor. A reader who believes the surplus capital will be returned should value the stock on the bull case, where the target is Rp20; a reader who believes the franchise reaches a mid-single-digit return should look at the same table and see that the target barely moves.

One inconsistency is worth stating rather than burying. Terminal growth of 4.0% with a sustainable ROE of 4.8% implies a payout of roughly one-sixth of earnings from the terminal year, while the model pays nothing through the forecast and the accumulated losses are not cleared for many years on the model's own cumulated profits [S7]. The direction is what matters: with the return below the cost of equity, a higher growth rate means more earnings retained at a below-cost return and therefore a lower multiple. A terminal growth rate consistent with a zero payout would be closer to the sustainable ROE itself, and it would produce a lower value still. So the 4.0% we use is the generous end of the range, and the target is already the better of the two defensible treatments.

The target is a price a minority holder could not trade at size. The construction is explicit: the justified-P/BV leg at 9.95 a share, weighted 65%, and the residual-income leg — floored at zero — weighted 35% give a blended value of 6.47, rolled forward at the cost of equity to the base target of 7.30. The probability-weighted scenario value is 10.33, and the engine applies a 10% liquidity discount, taking it to 9.29. The model also fails the house liquidity test, with average daily traded value of 849,443,657.1 rupiah and an investable flag of false [S0]. We disclose both rather than adjusting them away: a -91.1% call on a stock that trades this thinly is a statement about fundamental value, not a trade recommendation at size, and any position would have to be built and exited over weeks.

The regulatory risk is the most under-priced. OJK has said publicly that digital banks must build a sustainable model and not depend solely on affiliate support [S12]. Bank Raya's distribution, funding and customer acquisition all lean on BRI [S9], so a stricter reading of that principle — more independent funding, more standalone risk management, or higher capital for the digital model — would land directly on this bank. Likelihood is medium; impact is high, because the franchise is the affiliation.

The macro and funding risk is high and visible. System deposit growth outran loan growth in 2025 [S9], which means the marginal deposit is expensive and mobile; a bank with 35.8% CASA [S3] is less exposed than a wholesale-funded peer but still competes for rate-sensitive savings. If deposit costs reprice up while loan yields stay flat, the NIM path in the forecast does not happen and the ROE recovery slips by years. We treat this as medium likelihood and high impact.

The asset-quality risk is medium. Gross NPL is down to 2.5% [S3], but the low-quality stock is 19.3% and IDR1,087.3bn of loans are restructured [S7]. Restructured loans can migrate to non-performing when the modification ends, and the digital book — small-ticket loans to BRILink agents and micro-merchants — is unseasoned through a full credit cycle. Management says the digital NPL ratio is kept below a few per cent [S9]; the first test of that claim is the next two quarters of vintage data.

The operational and conduct risk is medium. The bank lends through agents and partners, which shortens the credit file and raises fraud and mis-selling risk, and the OJK statement on business models applies to exactly this kind of origination [S12]. A single large fraud event at a partner would hit both the P&L and the licence to grow.

The governance and control risk is medium. BRI owns 86.8% [S7], the free float is about 12.9% [S0], and 14.5% of loans are to related parties [S9]. A controlling shareholder can support the bank — and can also ask it to absorb group risk, fund group priorities, or raise equity at a price minority holders do not choose. The October 2026 board change is a reminder that the group sets the strategy [S6].

Liquidity risk is low. The bank holds a large securities and placement book, its liquidity ratios are far above the minimum, and its loan-to-deposit ratio is 78.1% [S5][S7]. The risk here is not a run; it is the opportunity cost of holding liquid assets that earn less than the cost of equity.

The supply risk is specific and dated. IDX has raised the minimum free float to fifteen per cent for listed companies, with a deadline in 2029 for issuers of this market capitalisation [S13]. The float here is about 12.9% [S0], so the controlling shareholder must place roughly two per cent of the share count, and the sale would land on a stock whose average daily traded value is 849,443,657.1 rupiah [S0]. We have not modelled it as a price shock, because we cannot know the placing price or the buyer, but it is a supply overhang with a date on it and it belongs in the bear case. It also cuts the other way on governance: a wider float improves liquidity and minority influence, and a strategic buyer taking the placing would be a positive.

Our bear case assumes credit cost stays near 5.6% as the digital vintage seasons, NIM gives back the deposit repricing, the recovery stream stops at the FY2025 level while fee income stays at its nine-month run-rate [S7], and the free-float overhang leaves the market demanding a higher return; the target is Rp7, with a probability of 25%. The base case is the forecast above and produces Rp7 at 50%. The bull case assumes cost of risk falls to the low end of the digital book's history, NIM keeps the mix benefit, the recovery stream persists and fee income builds, so terminal ROE reaches roughly seven per cent, and the required return falls as the franchise proves itself; the target is Rp20 at 25%. In both base and bear the residual-income leg floors at zero, so the blended value is not the justified-P/BV leg itself but only its 65% weight applied to it: 9.95 a share times that weight gives a blended value of 6.47, rolled forward at the cost of equity to the base target of 7.30. The residual-income method contributes nothing, and we disclose that concentration rather than present it as broad method agreement.

The bull is still below today's price, and that is the core of the call — but with a qualification the first version of this note got wrong. What the bull contains is a better operating franchise, not the capital return. A re-rating to the multiple a seven per cent return would warrant, or a distribution of the surplus at a target capital ratio, would each be worth several times the bull target; neither is in the numbers because neither is a forecast, and because the engine's bridge cannot reach a bank valuation method. A reader who wants to underwrite the corporate action should value the stock nearer book, and should do so with open eyes about who decides: BRI owns 86.8% of the shares [S7], the accumulated losses of IDR3,255.6bn mean any distribution needs a capital reduction rather than a dividend [S7][S8], and no such resolution is in the archive [S6]. That is the strongest case against us, stated plainly: if BRI decides to return the surplus, our target is wrong by a multiple of itself.

Signposts that would change our view: a credible capital-return plan (a capital reduction, a buyback at book, or a special dividend once losses are cleared); two or more quarters of credit cost at or below the digital book's through-cycle level; a sustained fall in the KKR stock; a funding mix shift that lifts CASA without buying it with promotions; and any OJK action on affiliate dependence that forces a change in the group's support. On the other side, a recovery line that halves without a fee offset and a float placement at a discount would each push us further down, and neither would surprise us.

Ownership is concentrated and stable. BRI holds 86.8% of the shares [S7], the public holds the rest, and the free float is about 12.9% [S0]. That float is thin enough that index inclusion and liquidity are constrained, and it fails the exchange's minimum: IDX now requires fifteen per cent free float, with a 2029 deadline for issuers of this size [S13], so a placement is a dated obligation rather than a hypothetical. It also means minority holders have little influence over capital decisions. We found no pledge of the controlling stake in the archived filings (checked); the group's support has historically been in the form of liquidity and funding rather than share pledges [S9].

The board is led by President Commissioner Muhamad Sidik Heruwibowo, with independent commissioners Retno Wahyuni Wijayanti and Johanes Kuntjoro Adisardjono [S9]. Management changed at the October 2026 RUPSLB [S6], and the new team's first full year will be the test of whether the digital plan is executed or merely restated. We treat board and management changes at a controlled bank as a group decision, not an independent signal.

The auditor is KAP Purwantono, Sungkoro & Surja, the Indonesian member firm of the EY network. The FY2025 accounts, the loss year that matters after the clean-up, were audited without qualification [S8] — that is the opinion we rely on, not the AGMS ratification of the prior year, which an earlier version of this note cited in error. The loss itself was disclosed and explained, and the deferred-tax write-off was the clean way to take the charge [S8]. There is no emphasis-of-matter paragraph in the archived accounts that changes our view of the balance sheet.

Related-party exposure is the main governance number. 14.5% of loans went to related parties at end-FY2025, with the balance at BRI itself a large part of the bank's placements [S9]. That is not automatically value-destroying — group lending can be better underwritten than standalone micro lending — but it means a meaningful share of the book is not priced by the market and its quality depends on the parent's standards. There is no dividend record to assess: the bank has not paid one, and the accumulated losses of IDR3,255.6bn explain why [S7][S8].

On ESG, the company's positives are financial inclusion — digital savings and small working-capital loans to micro-merchants and BRILink agents — and the governance certifications it discloses, including ISO certifications and a governance perception award [S5]. The negatives are conduct risk in agent-originated lending and the concentration of decision-making in a single controlling shareholder. Neither is a reason to avoid the stock on its own; both are reasons to demand a discount to the franchise value, which our method already does through the cost of equity.

The dated catalysts are the FY2026 close in December, the audited FY2026 results and FY2027 business plan in March, the annual RUPS in the second quarter, and the monthly OJK financial statements throughout [S7][S9]. The FY2026 close matters most: the market needs to see that Q4 does not repeat the FY2025 provisioning spike and that recovery income holds through the year [S8].

The KPIs we monitor between updates are the gross and net NPL ratios and the KKR stock [S7][S3]; the recovery line in the cash-flow statement, which is the swing factor in non-interest income [S7]; CASA and the cost of funds [S3]; digital outstanding and disbursement growth against the management target [S9]; the cost-to-income ratio on recurring income rather than reported income [S7]; the capital ratio and any capital action [S3]; and any OJK statement or action on affiliate dependence at digital banks [S12]. A quarter in which loans grow, NPL falls and recoveries normalise without a provision spike would be the first evidence that the base case is too cautious; we would revisit the sustainable-ROE assumption before we revisit the rating.

bear.narrative: The digital book seasons: cost of risk stays near 5% as the 2025-26 vintage ages, NIM gives back the deposit repricing, and the recovery stream stops at the FY2025 level while fee income stays at the Rp8bn nine-month run-rate [S7]. Provisions stay above pre-provision profit, equity erodes, and the IDX free-float rule forces supply into a float of about 13% by the 2029 deadline [S13], so the market demands a full illiquidity and overhang premium on a franchise that never earns its cost of capital. Because the engine holds the sustainable ROE at the base-case 4.75% in every scenario, the bear is expressed through the operating shocks plus a 100bp higher cost of equity, which is the market-price channel; the report discloses that limitation.

bull.narrative: Cost of risk falls to ~2% as the clean-up ends, NIM holds 40bp higher on a digital-heavy book and the recovery stream persists while fee income builds, so terminal ROE reaches about 7% and the warranted multiple roughly doubles. A proven franchise also compresses the required return by 100bp as the float normalises and the overhang premium goes. A capital return of about Rp49-77 a share at a 15-25% target CAR is the upside we still do not put in the numbers: it needs a shareholder resolution while accumulated losses of Rp3,255.6bn stand [S7], and the engine does not let a bridge item reach a bank method.

sensitivity.title: 12-month value vs NIM and credit cost
12-month value vs cost of equity and terminal growth

assumptions.label: Loan growth
assumptions.basis: The base case overrides management's own FY2026 RBB targets of +5%-6% loan growth, +2%-3% asset growth and +1%-2% deposit growth [S9] because the plan was overtaken by the accounts: gross loans fell from Rp7,715bn at December 2025 to Rp6,469bn at September 2026, -16.2% year-to-date, as the non-digital book is worked out, while digital outstanding still grew 11.3% yoy to Rp3,040bn [S7][S3]. We take the bottom of management's 2026 ranges where we cite them and otherwise use the run-rate. FY2026E -17.0% is the forecast that carries the nine-month rundown through the fourth quarter, not the year-to-date actual. FY2027E +1.0% is the crossover year: digital grows ~20% off Rp3.0tn while the residual legacy book halves. FY2028E-30E 11-12% is the digital franchise at the low end of its FY2025 run-rate (disbursement Rp28.8tn [S9]), not a market-share assumption - the bank is still shrinking its way to a smaller, better book.

assumptions.label: Deposit growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E -14.0% mirrors the loan rundown and the deliberate shedding of expensive time deposits: DPK was Rp9,540bn at December 2025 [S9] and the loan book is now 16% smaller, with LDR at 78.65% at September 2026 [S7]. FY2027E-30E 6-8% follows loans so LDR grinds from 78% to 83%; CASA at 35.83% [S3] and digital savings growing 35.6% yoy [S4] fund the mix rather than wholesale money.

assumptions.label: Earning assets / loans
assumptions.basis: The bank template computes total assets as the prior year grown at loan growth and earning assets as loans times this ratio, so the ratio must equal the last actual's total-assets-to-loans ratio for the balance sheet to articulate: Rp13,087bn of assets against Rp7,715bn of loans is 1.70x at December 2025 [S7][S10]. We hold 1.69x (earning assets at 99.6% of total assets; fixed assets, cash and intangibles are the rest) in every year, because the engine's total-assets line grows at loan growth and a constant ratio is the only internally consistent path. The consequence is stated in the report: with loans down 17% in FY2026E the total-assets proxy is smaller than the actual September-2026 balance sheet, where the securities and placement book absorbed the loan rundown (total assets Rp12,568bn [S7]).

assumptions.label: Net interest margin
assumptions.basis: FY2026E 5.95% is the 9M-2026 run-rate: reported NIM 5.83% [S7], 5.9% on the total-assets proxy, with interest expense down 10% yoy as high-cost deposits repriced. The path to 6.35% by FY2030E is mix, not price: digital loans (yield ~14%) rise from 47% to ~80% of the book and CASA from 36% to ~45%, worth ~0.4pp of margin; no policy-rate cut and no yield expansion on the legacy book is assumed.

assumptions.label: Non-interest income growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E +137% annualises the 9M-2026 run-rate, not fee income: non-interest income was Rp306.9bn in nine months against Rp167.2bn for all of FY2025, because the P&L recovery line alone was Rp276.7bn (Rp276.6bn in the cash-flow statement) versus Rp125.1bn in FY2025 [S7][S8]. Fee income is only Rp8.1bn in nine months [S7]. The line then runs off to about Rp196bn by FY2030E - the FY2025 recovery level of Rp125.1bn plus fee, commission and securities income of roughly Rp70bn - and is held flat (lt 0.0) because the LK does not disclose the recoverable written-off stock and a finite pool cannot grow in perpetuity. The base case is therefore not an annuity: the recovery stream is capitalised at the trough level, and the bear assumes it stops earlier while the bull assumes it persists longer.

assumptions.label: Cost-to-income
assumptions.basis: FY2026E 64.2% is the reported 9M-2026 cost-to-income ratio on total operating income: opex Rp561.3bn in nine months (personnel Rp260.9bn, promotion Rp73.1bn, other Rp227.4bn) against TOI Rp874.2bn [S7]. We hold the ratio near that level (64.2-64.8%) rather than letting it fall: the cost base is largely fixed - 766 staff [S0] and the O2O network do not scale down with the digital book - so as recovery income runs off, the ratio on recurring income stays high. The absolute cost path grows about 4% a year, which is the inflation rate the bank cannot avoid; the flat ratio is therefore a statement that costs cannot be cut as fast as the income mix changes, not that the bank wins operating leverage.

assumptions.label: Credit cost
assumptions.basis: FY2026E 5.58% is the 9M-2026 run-rate annualised: impairment of Rp295.7bn in nine months [S7] on average loans of about Rp7,059bn gives 5.58% for the full year. FY2027E 4.2% then 2.8% by FY2030E: gross NPL is already 2.53% and net 0.41% [S3], the digital book is kept below 3% [S9], and the remaining low-quality stock (KKR 19.34% [S7]) is the legacy tail being worked out, not new formation.

assumptions.label: Other items
assumptions.basis: Zero: no recurring non-operating items. The 9M-2026 non-operating line is Rp3.8bn of asset-sale and miscellaneous gains [S7], below the rounding of this model.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: Zero through the forecast, and the zero is an absence of taxable base rather than a tax holiday. The bank carried Rp3,255.6bn of accumulated losses at 30 September 2026 [S7] against cumulative pre-tax profit of roughly Rp1.5tn over FY2026E-35E on the model's own path, so the losses are not exhausted inside the horizon and no cash tax is paid. FY2025's reported tax was a Rp176.9bn deferred-tax derecognition, not a rate [S8]. The engine default of 11.4% would double-count that write-off against a loss-making base.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Zero: there are no minority interests on the consolidated balance sheet [S7]; the bank is 86.85% owned by BRI [S7] and consolidates no partly-owned subsidiary.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: Zero through the forecast. The bank posted a net loss of Rp498.6bn in FY2025 [S8] and carries accumulated losses against Rp3,011bn of equity [S7]; a dividend is barred until those are cleared. This is why the DDM weight is zero rather than a small payout assumption.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: Zero: no rights issue or buyback is in the archived record. A raise at 0.9x book would be dilutive and BRI has not announced one; the October 2026 RUPSLB changed management, not capital [S6].

assumptions.label: RWA / loans
assumptions.basis: 1.07x is calibrated to the last actual: CAR 42.35% on Rp2,937bn of equity implies RWA of ~Rp6.9tn against Rp6,469bn of loans [S3][S7]. It falls only as the digital book (lower risk weights on SME and consumer lending) displaces the legacy corporate book; we hold it flat, which keeps the capital ratio above 40% throughout and makes the excess-capital point visible.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth
assumptions.basis: 4% is the house IDR nominal terminal growth: below the 10-year sovereign (7.45%) and above long-run inflation, applied only after FY2030E when ROE has reached ~5.2%. With ROE below COE this is the assumption that does the most damage, so it is stated plainly rather than tuned.

challenges.challenge: Earning assets exceed total assets in every forecast year: FY2026E Rp12,295.1bn vs total assets Rp10,862.3bn (+13.2%) and FY2027E 12,741.5 vs 10,970.9 (+16.1%); deposits 8,204.4 plus equity 2,997.0 equals 11,201.4, already above total assets of 10,862.3. NII, the largest revenue line, is computed on an earning-asset base that cannot exist, and the forecast balance sheet does not articulate.
challenges.answer: Root cause traced to ea_loans: the template grows total assets at loan growth but scales earning assets at 1.92-1.97x loans, so EA exceeded TA. ea_loans is now 1.69 flat (the Dec-2025 TA/loans ratio) and EA is 99.6% of TA every year; FY2026E NII falls to 711.3, matching the ~712 the reviewer computed. The residual gap to the 9M run-rate is disclosed in section 3: the model's TA proxy shrinks with loans while the actual Sep-26 balance sheet is 12,567.6 with securities absorbing the rundown. [S7][S10]

challenges.challenge: The bull contains neither the re-rating nor the capital return §4 says it contains. §4 says the surplus-capital case 'is the bull case', and the bull narrative says ROE reaches 7% and the market re-rates to 0.3x book, but roe_sustainable is the fixed override 0.058 (fund record:209), so justified P/B stays 0.2011x in the bull; at 7% ROE the card's formula gives 0.335x BVPS = Rp39.8. The bull narrative itself says the capital return is 'the upside option we do not put in the numbers'. 'Even the bull case is below today's price' is therefore not established.
challenges.answer: The bull now carries a persisted recovery stream and a 100bp lower required return, and section 5 states plainly that the re-rating and the capital return are NOT in the numbers and why: the engine's scenario override accepts only val.coe/g/wacc and a bridge item does not reach a bank method. The Rp89/share figure is corrected to about Rp49-77 at a 15-25% target CAR. [S7][S13]

challenges.challenge: The bear shocks credit cost +60bp, NIM -40bp and loan growth -3pp but not the recovery line, which the report itself calls 'the swing factor in non-interest income' [S7]. With the justified-P/B leg fixed, the bear blended value is Rp15.5, of which Rp15.52 is the unchanged 0.20x P/B and Rp0.00 is residual income (floored at zero); the printed bear 'target' of Rp18 is 3% below the base.
challenges.answer: Bear now shocks a.noii_growth by -8pp so the recovery stream stops at the FY2025 level, mirrored by +8pp in the bull. Bear value falls to 6.63 against a 7.30 base, and section 5 discloses that the residual-income leg floors at zero by the engine's limited-liability rule. [S7]

challenges.challenge: 'Strip recoveries out and the core bank is still close to break-even' is contradicted by the filing: 9M-2026 PBT is Rp21.0bn and the recovery line is Rp276.6bn [S7], so recovery-stripped PBT is about -Rp255.5bn, roughly the size of the FY2025 loss. Even stripping only the year-on-year increment (276.6 vs 81.2 of other income) leaves about -Rp174bn.
challenges.answer: The sentence is withdrawn. The report now states that the 276.7bn recovery line is larger than the full-year profit before tax, so stripping it leaves the nine months at a loss of roughly the FY2025 size, and the correction is carried into the investment summary and section 3. [S7]

challenges.challenge: FY2026E books a net loss of Rp14.3bn while the actual 9M-2026 is a Rp21.0bn profit [S7]. Q4 is assumed to lose about Rp35bn on non-interest income falling from a 9M run-rate of Rp102bn a quarter to Rp55.9bn, with no source for a Q4 recovery stop. The calibration.roe justification attributes the near-zero year to the 5.35% cost of risk, but 9M provisions of Rp295.7bn [S7] left the bank profitable.
challenges.answer: FY2026E now runs at the 9M run-rate: non-interest income +137%, CTI 64.2% and credit cost 5.58% (9M impairment of 295.7 annualised), producing a small profit of 7.3 against the 9M actual of 21.0. The calibration justification is re-aligned to the reversal of the FY2025 charge, not the cost of risk. [S7][S8]

challenges.challenge: 65% of the value cannot move: roe_sustainable is an override of 0.058 that the engine returns unchanged in every scenario, so justified P/B is 0.2011x and Rp23.87 a share in base, bear and bull alike; only the 35% residual-income leg responds, and in the bear it is floored at zero (0.65 x 23.8746 = 15.5185 = the whole bear v0). The method set therefore cannot express either scenario §5 describes.
challenges.answer: roe_sustainable is no longer an override above the model: it is set to the model's own terminal ROE of 4.75%, so the primary P/B is driven by the forecast. A scenario-specific sustainable ROE is not possible in the engine (run_scenario accepts only val.coe/g/wacc), so scenarios move through the residual-income leg plus mirrored 100bp COE shocks, and section 5 discloses that the blend is the P/B leg in base and bear. [S7][S8]

challenges.challenge: The 5.8% sustainable ROE is 60bp above the highest ROE the model reaches in any year (FY2035E 5.30%) and its justification ('the mix shift continues after the forecast window') is contradicted by the model's flat FY2031E-35E path of 5.06-5.30%. At the model's FY2030E 5.2%, justified P/B is 0.134x = Rp15.9, not Rp23.9: the 'one notch' is worth about Rp8 a share of the primary method and about Rp6 of the target.
challenges.answer: The 5.8% override is withdrawn. roe_sustainable is now 4.75%, the FY2035E figure and the highest year the model produces, and the target is restated accordingly with the fragility of the multiple disclosed. [S7][S8]

challenges.challenge: §3 says the restated share count 'is the figure used for market capitalisation throughout', but model valuation market.mcap_rep is Rp1,147.6bn = Rp105 x 10,930m shares, the pack's erroneous count, not Rp2,597.8bn = Rp105 x 24,740.5m. The restatement reaches shares_m, EPS and BVPS but not mcap_rep, which the engine computes before the fact restatement.
challenges.answer: The section 3 sentence is corrected: the LK share count is used for EPS and book value per share, while the pack's market-cap field still uses its own count and should not be used. The report now says so and gives the corrected market capitalisation as price times the LK share count. [S8][S11]

challenges.challenge: History is still the pack's, not the LK's, although facts F7-F10 exist: model nii FY2024A 587.05 and FY2025A 712.64 vs LK 571.97 and 696.34 [S8]; noii 536.00 and 172.80 vs 529.96 and 167.23. §3's 'IDR536.0bn of non-interest income ... pre-provision profit of IDR483.8bn' is pack arithmetic; on the LK, FY2024 PPOP is Rp462.6bn and FY2025 CTI is the filing's 73.1% [S7], not 72.1%.
challenges.answer: The engine's restatement list does not include nii or noii, so F7-F10 cannot be wired into the history lines without an engine change. The report instead states the divergence explicitly, quoting the pack and LK figures side by side for FY2025 (712.6 vs 696.3 and 172.8 vs 167.2), and says it does not change the trend, the ROE path or the valuation. [S8][S0]

challenges.challenge: Base-case non-interest income never falls below Rp205.0bn (FY2030E) and is Rp250.0bn in FY2027E, yet the filing shows fee income of Rp8.125bn in 9M-2026, flat on 9M-2025 [S7]; the other roughly Rp240bn is recovery income capitalised for nine years and into the terminal with no sourced size for the written-off pool. The assumptions call the line 'cyclical, not annuity' and then model it as an annuity.
challenges.answer: Non-interest income is normalised: FY2026E annualises the 9M run-rate, then runs off to about 196 by FY2030E (the FY2025 recovery level of 125.1 plus fee and securities income of roughly 70) and is held flat. The LK does not disclose the recoverable written-off stock (checked in S7, S8 and S9), the resulting terminal ROE is 4.75% and the value is restated. [S7][S8]

challenges.challenge: A 10% liquidity discount is applied to the probability-weighted target (model valuation.liquidity_discount 0.10: tp_weighted 20.87 -> tp_final 18.78) and is not mentioned anywhere in the report. The same model shows the name failing the house liquidity gate (valuation.investable.ok=false, adtv=false; adtv_idr Rp849m a day). A -82% target on a stock that cannot be traded at size should say so.
challenges.answer: Section 4 now discloses the 10% liquidity discount, the weighted-to-final step from 10.3 to 9.3, the average daily traded value of 849m rupiah and the failed investable flag, and states that the target is a fundamental value a minority holder could not trade at size. [S0]

challenges.challenge: FY2026E loan growth of -17.0% departs by 22-23pp from management's own 2026 plan of +5-6% loan growth, +2-3% asset growth and +1-2% DPK growth [S9]. The basis cites the 9M run-rate but never acknowledges the plan it overrides, and fact F47 records the 2025 target column (5%-7%) as the FY2026E target (the 2026 column is 5%-6%); F49-F51 are also taken at the low end.
challenges.answer: The loan-growth basis now states that the base case overrides management's 2026 RBB targets of 5-6% loans, 2-3% assets and 1-2% deposits because gross loans fell 16% year-to-date, and the F47-F51 labels are corrected to the 2026 target column. [S9][S7]

challenges.challenge: The 4.0% terminal growth implies a payout of 1 - 4.0/5.8 = 31% from FY2036, while the model pays nothing through FY2035 and the Rp3,255.6bn accumulated loss at 30 Sep 2026 [S7] is not cleared until about FY2044 on the model's own cumulated profits (Rp1,530bn FY2027-35). The terminal value assumes a distribution the report says is legally barred.
challenges.answer: Section 4 states the inconsistency and its direction: 4% terminal growth implies a payout the model does not make, and because the return is below the cost of equity a higher growth rate lowers the multiple, so a zero-payout-consistent rate would give a lower value still; the 4% is the generous end. [S7]

challenges.challenge: 'The last audited accounts in the archive carried an unqualified opinion [S9]' cites the AGMS ratification of the FY2024 statements by KAP Purwantono, Sungkoro and Surja (10 March 2025), not the FY2025 audit, which is the one that matters after a Rp498.6bn loss. Separately, the §2 competitor list (Jago, Neo Commerce, DNAR, Bale, Superbank, SeaBank) is attributed to [S12], which discusses OJK's four digital-bank models and does not name them.
challenges.answer: Section 6 now cites the FY2025 unqualified audit opinion to the audited accounts in S8 and says explicitly that the AGMS ratification of the prior year is not the opinion relied on. The competitor list is no longer attributed to S12, which does not name those banks. [S8][S12]

challenges.challenge: The free float is 12.94% against an IDX minimum of 15% with a 2029 deadline (model konglo registry block: min_pct 15.0, compliant false, next_step_by 2029-03-31, source 'S25'), yet fund record has no S25 and the report never mentions the minimum. A forced float increase is unmodelled supply.
challenges.answer: The 15% free-float minimum and the 2029 deadline are cited to the registered S13, the supply overhang is in the bear narrative and in section 5 as a dated risk on a float of about 13%, and no S25 reference remains. [S13][S0]

FY2026E ROE of 0.24% is the same bank with the legacy book already written off: nine months of 2026 produced Rp21.0bn of profit before tax after Rp295.7bn of impairment, with gross NPL down from 14.02% to 2.53% [S7][S3]. The +15.7pp move is the reversal of the FY2025 charge, not a step-up in earnings power; the model then recovers only to 4.5% by FY2030E and 4.75% by FY2035E, so nothing optimistic is embedded in the jump.

flags.message: expected return -91%: name the two or three sourced drivers that produce it and what today's price implies (reverse DCF)
flags.justification: Three sourced drivers produce the -91%: (1) a clean-up-normalised ROE that never reaches the 12.95% cost of equity, peaking at 4.75% in FY2035E on a 64.8% cost-to-income ratio and 2.8% credit cost [S7][S8], which on the house warranted-multiple formula is 0.08x book; (2) Rp3,255.6bn of accumulated losses mean the payout is zero through the forecast, so the DDM is zero by construction and no cash reaches a minority holder [S7]; (3) the recovery line that carries the P&L (Rp276.7bn in nine months, Rp125.1bn in FY2025) is a finite, undisclosed pool, so we normalise it rather than capitalise the run-rate [S7][S8]. What the price implies: at 0.88x book [S0] the market capitalises a sustainable ROE near the cost of equity or a capital return. The engine's reverse DCF cannot bracket the price on any combination of NIM and credit cost it can vary - only a corporate action or a franchise return at the cost of equity gets to Rp105, and neither is in the accounts.

flags.message: method weights differ from the industry default {'justified_pbv': 0.5, 'residual_income': 0.3, 'ddm': 0.2}
flags.justification: The DDM weight is zero because the payout is zero for the whole forecast while Rp3,255.6bn of accumulated losses stand, so a dividend discount model would value the bank at zero by construction rather than by analysis [S7][S8]. Residual income keeps 0.35 because it is the only leg that re-runs the model under each scenario and the house card calls residual income inapplicable on near-zero earnings rather than wrong [S7]. Justified P/BV carries the balance as the card's digital-bank variant prescribes once the bank is profitable, and the engine's PE and PBV cross-checks are meaningless at a 0.2% ROE [S8].
